## Overview

In this graded assignment, you will practice with Unix shell commands,
especially the "data tools" commands, and with Git commands.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday September 27^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**:
  Same as for GA1.
  That is, you don't need to submit anything or notify the instructors:
  we will look for files, which you'll create as part of the assignment,
  in the appropriate location at OSC.
  (We can also see when the files were last modified.)

### Academic integrity

::: callout-important
### Gen-AI check

- For this assignment, you are allowed to search the internet, consult books,
  and so on, but not to use generative AI
  (so you cannot use, for example, **Google AI Mode** output).

- **If you use commands or code constructs that we did not cover in class**,
  then you must provide the source: webpage or book page, etc.
  Alternatively, you can argue that you already knew the command in question
  from previous self-study or experience.
  If you don't provide a source or otherwise explain your usage of such commands,
  your answer will be considered wrong and not give you any points.
:::

### Rubric

You can earn a maximum of 0.5 points for each of the numbered 20 questions/items below.
There is a bonus 21^st^ question that can earn you 1 point if you dropped points elsewhere.

## Detailed steps

### General

- Execute Unix shell and Git commands to answer all questions unless explicitly
  instructed otherwise (e.g., step 1 below).

- Whenever you issue a command in the terminal, make sure to include the command
  in a Markdown code block, and also include the output of the command in another
  Markdown code block --- same way as for [GA1](/GA/GA1.qmd).

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
  ### A worked example of how to answer a question when you ran a command _(Click to expand)_

  **Assignment questions:**

  1. Print your current working directory to screen.
  2. Print the current date and time to screen.

  **Your answers as part of your Markdown document:**

  ````bash-in-nocolor
  ### 1: Print your current working directory to screen

  ```bash
  # Print the path to the dir I am currently in
  pwd
  ```

  The output of the command was:

  ```
  /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer
  ```

  ### 2: Print the current date and time to screen

  ```bash
  # Print the current date and time
  date
  ```

  The output of the command was:

  ```
  Fri Sep 11 14:30:00 EDT 2026
  ```

  ````
  <hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
  :::

- **Exception for Git commands**:
  for the questions that only ask you to initialize a repository or to stage and
  commit files (questions 02, 03, 12, and 20),
  you don't need to include the commands or their output in your README:
  we will check your Git repository directly.
  Do include your `git status` commands, their output, and your answers
  for questions 11 and 14.

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code (`Code Server`) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual,
  and open a terminal in that session.

- Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA2`,
  and navigate there. **This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.**
  Inside it, also create a dir `data` and a dir `results`.

- In your working dir, create a `README.md` file and open it in the VS Code editor.
  Use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers.

### Part A: Starting a Git repository

01. Add a header to your README file to indicate that this file (and dir) is for
    your assignment.

02. Initialize a Git repository inside your new directory.

03. Add & stage and then commit the README file with an appropriate commit message.

### Part B: Exploring the GTF file with Unix data tools

04. Copy the genome annotation GTF file `annot.gtf.gz` that is in your
    copy of the @garrigós2025 data to a file `data/annot.gtf.gz`
    (i.e., into the `data` dir you just created).

05. Check the file size of `annot.gtf.gz`.
    Then, decompress the GTF file with the `gunzip` command below.
    Finally, check the size of the resulting `annot.gtf` file.
    Roughly how many times larger is the uncompressed file than the compressed file?

    ```bash
    gunzip data/annot.gtf.gz
    ```

06. The total number of "genomic features" (genes, exons, etc.)
    listed in a GTF file is simply the number of lines in its main/table section.
    Count the total number of lines in `annot.gtf`,
    then look at file contents to count the number of header lines by eye.
    What count do you get?

07. Let's do the above line count in a more automated way.
    Based on your knowledge of what the GTF header lines look like,
    combine `grep -v` and `wc -l` to count the number of genomic features in the file.
    What count do you get?

08. Did you get the same count in questions 6 and 8?
    If not, can you figure out why they might differ?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints_</summary>

    - The manual count was off: you missed a line that is not a header line but
      also does not contain any genomic feature.

    - So the question boils down to: which line(s) other than the header
      lines contain the pattern you used with `grep` above?

    - Review the "Additional `grep` tips" box in
      [the section on `grep`](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#grep-to-print-lines-that-match-a-pattern)
      to find an option that might help you make sense of that.
    </details>

09. How many distinct "sequences" (chromosome/scaffolds/contigs) are represented
    in the annotation file?
    Store a list of these distinct sequences in a file `results/scaffolds.txt`.
    _(This gives an idea of the quality of the genome assembly:_
    _a high-quality assembly will have only a few sequences, ideally one per chromosome.)_

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint_</summary>
    In this and all following questions, you'll only want to consider the table
    part of the file, so you should start your commands with `grep -v` as above.
    </details>

10. Print a "count table" (like we did towards the end of
    [this section](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#combining-cut-sort-and-uniq-to-create-a-list))
    of feature types in the annotation:
    this should have a count of the number of times each feature type occurs.
    _(Such a table will for example show how many genes have been annotated in this genome_
    _-- quite useful!)_

11. A labmate wants to know how many genes have been annotated in this genome,
    and runs the command below, which returns `408397`.

    ```bash
    grep -c "gene" data/annot.gtf
    ```

    Which of the following statements is true?

    a) This is the correct number of genes.
    b) This overcounts the number of genes, because the word "gene" also occurs
       in other lines than those for genes.
    c) This undercounts the number of genes, because `grep` only matches whole words.
    d) This command gives an error, because the file is tab-delimited.

    Run the command to confirm your answer.
    Then, write and run a command that does return the correct number of genes
    as a single number.

12. Check the status of your Git repository.
    You should see that your `README` has changed but also that Git has detected
    the files in the `data` and `results` dirs.
    You don't want to commit any files in the `data` and `results` dirs,
    so create a `.gitignore` file that makes Git ignore them.
    Check the status of your repository again --
    is your `.gitignore` file working as intended?

13. Stage and commit the `.gitignore` file.
    Then, in a separate commit, stage and commit the `README.md` file again.

### Part C: Exploring the FASTQ files with Unix data tools

14. Copy the FASTQ file `S63_R1.fastq.gz` of the @garrigós2025 data
    into your `data` dir (keep the original name).

15. Check the status of your Git repository. Does the FASTQ file show up? Why/why not?

16. How many reads does the FASTQ file contain?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for hints_</summary>
    Recall from the [week 4 exercises](../week04/w4_exercises.qmd)
    that a direct linecount of the compressed file will **not** give you the correct answer.
    Also, don't forget to convert the number of lines to the number of reads.
    </details>

17. How many reads in the FASTQ file contain the sequence `ACGT`?
    _(You can assume this string does not occur outside of the lines that contain DNA sequences.)_

18. How many reads in the FASTQ file contain at least 10 consecutive `N`s ---
    i.e., uncalled bases?
    _(You can assume that stretches of N's do not occur in the sequence quality lines.)_

19. Compare the number of 35-bp reads from the previous question
    with the number of reads with at least 10 consecutive `N`s from question 16.
    What does this seem to tell you?
    To confirm, can you check what a sample of 35-bp reads look like?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for hints_</summary>
    To see the sequences in the 35-bp reads,
    use a `grep` option that allows you to see the line after each match along
    with the matching line.
    Also, pipe `grep`'s output to `less` or `head` to avoid having thousands of
    lines printed to screen.
    </details>

20. Stage and commit the `README.md` file again.

### Bonus

21. Name at least two concepts or commands that we have gone over in the course
    so far, but which you feel you do not (fully) understand.
    It helps to be specific about what you struggle with.
